title: Leaders as Mediators When Team Members Are in Conflict
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece lays out what it takes for a leader to step out of their authority role and mediate conflict between two team members instead of simply ordering it to stop. It warns that using positional power to demand resolution usually drives conflict underground rather than resolving it. Instead, the leader is asked to become a neutral third party, guarantee confidentiality, and probe both sides' accounts under a strict 'no blame or shame' rule. The goal isn't to assign fault but to help both parties build a workable agreement for coexisting going forward.
points: Demanding that a conflict be settled through positional authority typically drives it underground rather than resolving it.
To mediate effectively, a leader must suspend their role as boss and act as an objective third party.
Confidentiality has to be established up front so both parties will speak freely.
A 'no blame or shame' ground rule keeps both sides from turning the mediation into a fresh fight.
The goal of mediation is a workable agreement for coexisting, not a verdict on who was right.
quotes: If the team members fear retribution for their struggle, they simply go underground and work to interfere with each other at every turn.
For a leader to mediate a conflict, they must suspend their role as leader and take on the role of an objective third party.
The ground rule of “no blame or shame” must be in place and enforced by the leader.
No one has to be declared right or wrong. A mutually agreeable solution doesn’t require it.
Good leaders play many different roles. When it comes to mediating conflict, sometimes they are just an objective third party.
